headline_segments.why: Just the subject; not a red flag.

Not a red flag on its own.

body_segments.value: Get in touch with your zen
and picking up some Ashwagandha supplements on your way out
body_segments.why: @healthguru sells supplements from their yoga studio; there is a financial motive (Poster signal).
Just naming the supplement — not a red flag.

questions.explanation: 'GUARANTEED' is an overclaim (Language signal), and the yoga-studio-selling-supplements framing is a financial conflict of interest (Poster signal). Naming the Journal of Public Health isn't itself a red flag — the real issue is that no DOI or link is provided.

questions.prompt: Drag each element of this post into the correct signal bucket.

post.study_preview: Effects of Acute Ashwagandha Ingestion on Cognitive Function — Looks like an official study…
post.body: Ashwagandha has been shown to improve your focus, attention, and clarity of mind. If you're struggling with attention or focus, ashwagandha might help.

draggables.text: Study screenshot with no clickable DOI
draggables.why: A screenshot can be fabricated, cropped, or outdated. Without a clickable DOI or PubMed ID, it cannot be verified.

draggables.text: "has been shown to improve your focus"
draggables.why: 'Has been shown' is an overclaim compared to hedged wording like 'suggests' or 'may support'.
'Might help' is properly hedged language — that's how honest science actually talks.
No institutional affiliation, no listed credentials. Anonymous wellness accounts warrant skepticism.

questions.explanation: A screenshot is not the same as a verifiable source. Strong language and anonymous posters are red flags. Hedged language like 'might help' is fine.

questions.prompt: Rate this post from Fake to Credible, then select every signal that is a red flag.

post.headline: Science has PROVEN that Vitamin D cures immune deficiencies. Doctors don't want you to know this!
post.body: @dr.wellness_official: I've researched this for years. Trust the science!

signals.label: Source: no study or journal linked
signals.why: 'I've researched this' is not evidence. No DOI, no journal, no study linked.

signals.label: Language: 'proven' and 'cures' are overclaims
signals.why: Science says 'suggests', 'is associated with', 'may reduce risk'. 'Proven' and 'cures' are red flags.

signals.label: Language: conspiracy framing ('doctors don't want you to know')
signals.why: Conspiracy framing is designed to pre-empt skepticism. It's a manipulation tactic.

signals.label: Poster: 'dr.' in the username means this is a credible expert
signals.why: Anyone can put 'dr.' in a handle. Verify through institutional affiliation, not the username.

questions.explanation: This post is clearly fake. No source linked, multiple language red flags (absolutes + conspiracy framing), and 'dr.' in a handle is not a real credential.

post.headline: NEW research from Harvard confirms: 10mg melatonin nightly resets your circadian rhythm and CURES insomnia.
post.body: I've been sleeping 8 hours straight every night since I started. Link in bio for the supplement we recommend.

questions.why: "Cures" is an overclaim and "Harvard" is name-dropped without a study link. Personal anecdote isn't evidence, and the affiliate link signals financial motive.

post.headline: Soberg et al., Cell Reports Medicine, 2021. doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2021.100408
post.body: Repeated cold exposure may improve glucose tolerance in some adults. Effects were small and varied across participants. More research needed in larger populations.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed source with a DOI, hedged language ("may improve," "small," "varied"), neutral institutional poster, and the post acknowledges its own limitations.

post.headline: Seed oils literally cause inflammation in your body.
post.body: Studies show linoleic acid is the #1 driver of chronic disease. That's why I switched my whole family to tallow and never looked back. Big Food doesn't want you to know this.

questions.why: "Literally cause" is an overclaim, "studies show" with no citation is empty rhetoric, the conspiracy framing ("Big Food doesn't want you to know") is a manipulation tactic, and the poster is an anonymous lifestyle account with no credentials.

post.headline: A 2023 NEJM study PROVED that intermittent fasting REVERSES type 2 diabetes in 6 weeks.
post.body: If you're pre-diabetic and not doing 16:8, you're choosing to stay sick. The science is settled.

questions.why: "Proved" and "reverses" are overclaims — the actual NEJM intermittent fasting research shows mixed, modest effects, not 6-week reversals. "The science is settled" is rhetorical absolutism, and the 2023 NEJM study is named but not actually cited.

post.headline: Recent research suggests creatine may modestly improve memory in sleep-deprived adults.
post.body: Effects appear strongest in vegetarians and people under cognitive load. Standard 5g/day.

questions.why: The language is properly hedged ("may," "modestly," "appears") and the claim is roughly consistent with real research, but no study or DOI is linked. Hedged language without a verifiable source is still an unverifiable claim, and "@dr.evidence" is an anonymous handle (anyone can put "dr." in front).

post.headline: IV vitamin C therapy may support immune resilience in some adults.
post.body: Citation: a 2024 review in Mayo Clinic Proceedings [https://mcpress.mayoclinic.org/living-well/iv-vitamin-therapy-understanding-the-lack-of-proven-benefit-and-potential-risks-of-this-health-fad/]. Book your drip at our Manhattan clinic.

questions.why: Hedged language, plausible-sounding source, sounds careful, but the poster is a clinic that sells the exact treatment they're citing. Even when sources and language pass the test, a direct financial stake in your conclusion is a red flag (Poster signal).

post.headline: Estruch et al., NEJM, 2018. doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800389
post.body: Adherence to a Mediterranean diet was associated with a ~30% relative reduction in major cardiovascular events in high-risk adults over ~5 years. Findings are observational at the diet level; effect sizes vary by population.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed primary source with a DOI from a top-tier journal, hedged language ("associated with," "observational," "vary by population"), institutional poster with no commercial interest. The post acknowledges its own methodological limits.

post.headline: Sunscreen is causing the skin cancer epidemic, not preventing it.
post.body: The chemicals are toxic. Dermatologists won't admit it because they're paid by Big Pharma. Use coconut oil and get sunlight.

questions.why: Conspiracy framing ("won't admit it," "Big Pharma") is a manipulation tactic that pre-empts skepticism. The claim contradicts decades of dermatology research, no source is cited, and an anonymous "truth community" account has no expertise.

post.headline: New study: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG may reduce stress markers in healthy adults [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30741841/].
post.body: Try our 12-strain Gut Balance blend: formulated with research-backed probiotics. 20% off this week.

questions.why: The cited research on L. rhamnosus GG is real and properly hedged, but the seller's product is a different 12-strain blend that may not contain L. rhamnosus GG at clinical doses. Citing real research to sell a different product is a classic poster-bias tactic.

post.headline: Cold plunges boost dopamine 250% (Stanford).
post.body: I do 3 minutes at 38°F every morning. Mood, focus, energy: completely different person. Don't sleep on this.

questions.why: "Stanford" is name-dropped without a citation, and the "250%" figure is actually a misrepresentation, and no explanation is given for this figure. Also the post generalizes transient dopamine elevation as a daily life-outcome metric. Personal anecdote is presented as evidence.

post.headline: The carnivore diet REVERSED my autoimmune disease in 90 days.
post.body: Doctors said I'd be on medication for life. They were wrong. The results speak for themselves: try it for 30 days and tell me I'm crazy.

questions.why: A single anecdote isn't evidence, no clinical source supports the broader claim, and the "doctors were wrong" framing pre-empts medical skepticism. "Reversed" is an overclaim; chronic conditions rarely reverse from dietary change alone.

post.headline: Bouillon et al., Endocrine Reviews, 2019. doi.org/10.1210/er.2018-00126
post.body: Vitamin D supplementation appears to provide modest benefits primarily in adults with documented deficiency. Routine supplementation in vitamin-D-replete adults shows little to no clinical effect in most outcomes studied.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed source with a DOI, properly hedged language ("appears," "modest," "little to no"), institutional government poster, and the post deliberately distinguishes between deficient and replete populations rather than promoting blanket use.

post.headline: If you have anxiety, brain fog, headaches, fatigue, or trouble sleeping, you're probably magnesium deficient.
post.body: Our triple-blend magnesium fixes all of it in 7 days. Use code RELAX20 for 20% off.

questions.why: A single supplement claimed to fix five different symptoms is a textbook overgeneralization. "Probably deficient" with no diagnostic basis, "fixes all of it in 7 days" is an overclaim, and the discount code makes the financial motive explicit.

post.headline: A 2024 study confirms what we've known for years: seed oils trigger heart disease at the cellular level.
post.body: Linoleic acid oxidizes inside arterial walls. Switch to butter, ghee, or tallow. Your future self will thank you.

questions.why: "A 2024 study" with no journal, authors, or DOI cannot be verified. The mechanistic claim oversimplifies decades of contested research on linoleic acid. "Ancestral_md" is credential mimicry, anyone can use "md" in a handle.

post.headline: Drysdale et al., Sleep Medicine Reviews, 2023. doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2023.101764
post.body: Meta-analysis of 24 studies: caffeine within ~9 hours of bedtime may meaningfully reduce sleep quality on average. Individual sensitivity varies widely: some people are unaffected, others should cut off earlier.

questions.why: Peer-reviewed meta-analysis with a DOI, hedged language ("may," "on average," "varies widely"), and the post explicitly acknowledges individual variation rather than prescribing a one-size-fits-all rule.
